Sonic the Hedgehog characters.Pac-Man: A yellow circle who eats dots, and he appeared alongside Sonic in Smash Bros. Ultimate.
Sonic the Hedgehog characters.Donkey Kong: A large ape and Nintendo star, who began as a villain who was beaten by Mario.
Sonic the Hedgehog characters.Diddy Kong: Donkey Kong's chimp sidekick, who debuted in Donkey Kong Country in 1994.
Sonic the Hedgehog characters.Rayman: A limbless hero from Ubisoft, created in 1995 by Michel Ancel, and well known for his floating hands.
Sonic the Hedgehog characters.Ratchet: A lombax mechanic from Insomniac Games, who works with a robot named Clank.

Parts of a tennis court.Net: It stands 3 ft 6 in at the posts and 3 ft at the centre. Players who touch it while the ball is in play lose the point.
Parts of a tennis court.Baseline: The back boundary of the court, and lines count as in, so a ball touching it is good.
Parts of a tennis court.Service line: Marks the back edge of the service boxes, 21 feet from the net, and a serve landing past it is a fault.
Parts of a tennis court.Tramlines: The two side strips used only in doubles. British fans call them tramlines after tram tracks.
Parts of a tennis court.Net post: When singles is played on a doubles court, singles sticks hold the net up at the narrower width.
Parts of a tennis court.Centre mark: A small line in the middle of the baseline that tells the server not to stray across the middle when serving.
Parts of a tennis court.Service box: Where a serve must land, one on each side. They're known as the deuce and ad courts.
Parts of a tennis court.Umpire's chair: The tall chair gives the umpire a clear view over the net and across both lines of the court.
Parts of a tennis court.Doubles alley: Another name for the strip between singles and doubles sidelines, 4.5 ft wide, used only in doubles.
Parts of a tennis court.Crease: Hockey and cricket both have a crease, but a tennis court doesn't, so it's a trap.
Parts of a tennis court.Dugout: Baseball's sunken shelter for players, a place nothing resembles on a tennis court.
Parts of a tennis court.End zone: Football's scoring area, ten yards deep, and nothing like a tennis court's markings.
Parts of a tennis court.Penalty spot: Soccer's spot for penalties, 12 yards from the goal, with no equivalent on a tennis court.
Parts of a tennis court.Hog line: Curling's line that stones must cross to stay in play, not a tennis feature.
Parts of a tennis court.Oche: Darts' throw line, 7 feet 9.25 inches from the board, from a pub game and not a tennis court.
Parts of a tennis court.Free-throw line: Basketball's line, 15 feet from the backboard, from a different court entirely.
Parts of a tennis court.Fairway: The cut grass between a golf tee and green, not part of a tennis court, even a grass one at Wimbledon.
Parts of a tennis court.Pitcher's mound: Baseball's raised mound, 60 feet 6 inches from home plate, with no tennis equivalent.
Parts of a tennis court.Corner flag: Soccer's flag at each corner of the pitch, not found on a tennis court.
Parts of a tennis court.Blue line: Ice hockey's zone dividers, painted on the ice, which don't exist on a tennis court.
Parts of a tennis court.Tee box: The golf area where each hole begins, which is no part of a tennis court.
Parts of a tennis court.Goalposts: Football and rugby posts, tall goal structures that tennis doesn't have.
Parts of a tennis court.Faceoff circle: Hockey's circles where play restarts, nothing tennis has.
Parts of a tennis court.Hack: Curling's rubber foothold embedded in the ice, not a tennis feature.

Chess engines and computers.Deep Blue: IBM's computer beat world champion Garry Kasparov in a 1997 match, the first time a machine won a match against a reigning champion.
Chess engines and computers.Stockfish: A free, open-source engine that has won many computer chess championships and has been used by millions to analyse games.
Chess engines and computers.AlphaZero: A DeepMind program that taught itself chess in about nine hours by playing itself, and then beat Stockfish in a 2017 match.
Chess engines and computers.Leela Chess Zero: A community-run, open-source project inspired by AlphaZero that learns by self-play and has won top engine events.
Chess engines and computers.Komodo: A top chess engine co-created by Don Dailey and Larry Kaufman, and it won several world computer chess championships in the 2010s.
Chess engines and computers.Houdini: A strong engine that dominated computer chess in the early 2010s, and its name is a nod to the escape artist.
Chess engines and computers.Fritz: A chess program that beat world champion Vladimir Kramnik in 2006, and it also became a popular product for learners.
Chess engines and computers.Rybka: A chess engine from International Master Vasik Rajlich that dominated from 2007, and later stripped of titles over code plagiarism.
Chess engines and computers.Shredder: A German chess engine by Stefan Meyer-Kahlen that won several world computer chess championships, including four in a row in the 1990s and 2000s.
Chess engines and computers.Siri: Apple's voice assistant arrived in 2011, and it's a general assistant, not a chess machine.
Chess engines and computers.Alexa: Amazon's voice assistant, and the name was reportedly inspired by the ancient library of Alexandria.
Chess engines and computers.Watson: IBM's computer won on Jeopardy! in 2011, and a trivia champion, not a chess one.
Chess engines and computers.AlphaGo: The DeepMind program beat Lee Sedol at Go in 2016, a game thought to be far harder for computers than chess.
Chess engines and computers.Cortana: Microsoft's assistant named after an AI in the Halo video games, not a chess engine.
Chess engines and computers.Clippy: The paperclip helper in Microsoft Office who asked if you were writing a letter, and he never played chess.
Chess engines and computers.R2-D2: A droid in Star Wars, and he beeps through the movies as a fictional character.
Chess engines and computers.WALL-E: The tiny trash-compacting robot from the 2008 Pixar film, and not a chess player.
Chess engines and computers.Roomba: A robotic vacuum cleaner sold since 2002, and it wanders about the floor rather than a chessboard.
Chess engines and computers.Tamagotchi: A virtual pet from 1996 Japan, and a toy to be fed rather than a chess opponent.
Chess engines and computers.Furby: A talking toy that took the 1998 holiday season by storm, and it has no chess skills.
Chess engines and computers.KITT: The talking car in the 1980s show Knight Rider, a fictional sidekick and not a chess engine.
Chess engines and computers.Optimus Prime: The Autobot leader from Transformers, a fictional truck-turned-robot, and no chess computer.
Chess engines and computers.Baymax: The soft inflatable healthcare robot in Big Hero 6, and a Disney character.
Chess engines and computers.Bender: The foul-mouthed, cigar-smoking robot from Futurama, a bending unit by trade and not a chess player.

Titles for a reigning monarch.King: The classic title of a male monarch, from Old English. It's used in dozens of nations, past and present.
Titles for a reigning monarch.Queen: A female sovereign or a king's wife. Queen regnant, such as Elizabeth II, rules in her own right.
Titles for a reigning monarch.Pharaoh: Egypt's ruler. The word originally meant 'great house', and referred to the palace not the king.
Titles for a reigning monarch.Tsar: The Russian emperor's title, derived from the Roman 'Caesar'. The last tsar, Nicholas II, was overthrown in 1917.
Titles for a reigning monarch.Sultan: Ruler of an Islamic state, notably the Ottoman Empire, where the sultan reigned for around six centuries.
Titles for a reigning monarch.Emperor: A ruler of an empire, from Latin imperator, a commander of armies. Rome, Japan and Ethiopia all used the word.
Titles for a reigning monarch.Kaiser: German emperor, also from 'Caesar'. The last Kaiser, Wilhelm II, abdicated at the end of World War I.
Titles for a reigning monarch.Shah: The Persian word for king. Iran's last one was toppled in 1979, ending 2,500 years of tradition.
Titles for a reigning monarch.Khan: A Mongol and Turkic ruler's title, used by Genghis Khan, and later 'Great Khan', ruling over huge territory.
Titles for a reigning monarch.Maharaja: Trap: not here, but a real royal title: 'great king' in India, used by princes who ruled states until 1947.
Titles for a reigning monarch.Emir: A Muslim ruler or commander. It gave the Spanish word 'almirante' and English 'admiral'.
Titles for a reigning monarch.Negus: The title of Ethiopia's emperor, and it means 'king'. Haile Selassie held it until 1974, when he was deposed.
Titles for a reigning monarch.President: Trap: an elected leader, not a monarch. Presidents serve terms rather than reign for life.
Titles for a reigning monarch.Prime Minister: Trap: Britain's PM, appointed to lead the government, not a king or queen. The monarch is separate.
Titles for a reigning monarch.Chancellor: Trap: Germany's head of government is a Chancellor, elected by parliament and not a hereditary ruler.
Titles for a reigning monarch.Mayor: Trap: a city leader, usually elected. Even in the Middle Ages, mayors served under kings, never as one.
Titles for a reigning monarch.Consul: Trap: in ancient Rome, two consuls shared power for a year, the opposite of a single reigning monarch.
Titles for a reigning monarch.Vizier: Trap: a high official serving a caliph or sultan. The vizier ran the government, but the ruler held the throne.
Titles for a reigning monarch.Governor: Trap: someone who runs a province or state on behalf of a higher authority, not a sovereign.
Titles for a reigning monarch.Sheriff: Trap: a county law officer. The word comes from 'shire reeve', and he was appointed by the king, never a king himself.
Titles for a reigning monarch.Senator: Trap: a lawmaker in a legislature, elected or appointed. The word comes from Latin for 'old man', but not a monarch.
Titles for a reigning monarch.Archbishop: Trap: a senior bishop in the church. The Archbishop of Canterbury crowns English monarchs, but isn't one.
Titles for a reigning monarch.General: Trap: a military rank, high but still under a ruler's command. Many generals have seized power, but title and crown are not the same.
Titles for a reigning monarch.Admiral: Trap: a high naval rank, whose name comes from the Arabic 'amir', meaning a commander. It is not a monarch.

Enlightenment thinkers.Voltaire: Pen name of François-Marie Arouet, who defended religious tolerance and free speech and mocked optimism in his satire Candide.
Enlightenment thinkers.Rousseau: Jean-Jacques Rousseau opened The Social Contract with 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains', a line that fed the French Revolution.
Enlightenment thinkers.John Locke: This English philosopher argued that people hold natural rights to life, liberty and property, ideas that echo through the American Declaration of Independence.
Enlightenment thinkers.Montesquieu: His The Spirit of the Laws proposed splitting government into legislative, executive and judicial branches, a model copied in the US Constitution.
Enlightenment thinkers.Kant: Immanuel Kant answered 'What is Enlightenment?' with the motto 'Dare to know', and he reportedly walked so punctually that neighbors set clocks by him.
Enlightenment thinkers.Diderot: Denis Diderot edited the Encyclopédie, a huge French reference work of 28 volumes meant to gather all human knowledge and spread reason.
Enlightenment thinkers.David Hume: This Scottish skeptic argued we never actually observe cause and effect, only events that follow one another, which later woke Kant from his 'dogmatic slumber'.
Enlightenment thinkers.Adam Smith: Another Scot, he wrote The Wealth of Nations in 1776 and described the market's 'invisible hand'. He was a moral philosopher before being called an economist.
Enlightenment thinkers.Mary Wollstonecraft: Her 1792 A Vindication of the Rights of Woman argued that women only seem inferior because they are denied education. Her daughter wrote Frankenstein.
Enlightenment thinkers.Condorcet: A French mathematician who championed votes for women and the abolition of slavery, he also found the voting paradox that bears his name.
Enlightenment thinkers.Plato: Trap: he is an ancient Greek, about 2,000 years before the Enlightenment. His Academy in Athens lasted for centuries, but he belongs to classical antiquity.
Enlightenment thinkers.Aristotle: Trap: a student of Plato in the 4th century BC, so classical, not Enlightenment. Enlightenment thinkers often rebelled against his authority in science.
Enlightenment thinkers.Socrates: Trap: ancient Athens, over 2,000 years earlier. He wrote nothing himself, so we know him through Plato, and he was executed in 399 BC.
Enlightenment thinkers.Confucius: Trap: this Chinese sage lived around 500 BC. His teachings on ethics and duty shaped East Asia, and some Enlightenment thinkers admired them from afar.
Enlightenment thinkers.Machiavelli: Trap: he wrote The Prince around 1513, in the Renaissance, long before the Enlightenment. His name became shorthand for ruthless political cunning.
Enlightenment thinkers.Thomas Aquinas: Trap: a 13th-century Italian friar who blended Aristotle with Christian theology. He is a medieval scholastic, the sort of tradition the Enlightenment challenged.
Enlightenment thinkers.Nietzsche: Trap: he came after the Enlightenment, in the late 1800s. He famously declared 'God is dead' and criticized the faith in reason his predecessors had.
Enlightenment thinkers.Kierkegaard: Trap: a 19th-century Danish thinker often called the father of existentialism, writing well after the Enlightenment, and he distrusted its pure rationalism.
Enlightenment thinkers.Sartre: Trap: a 20th-century French existentialist who declined the 1964 Nobel Prize in Literature. Far too late for the Age of Reason.
Enlightenment thinkers.Augustine: Trap: bishop of Hippo around AD 400, author of Confessions. A late-antique Christian thinker, roughly 1,300 years before the Enlightenment.
Enlightenment thinkers.Seneca: Trap: a Roman Stoic who tutored the emperor Nero, then died on Nero's orders in AD 65. Ancient, not Enlightenment.
Enlightenment thinkers.Marcus Aurelius: Trap: a Roman emperor and Stoic whose private journal, now called Meditations, was never meant for publication. He ruled in the 2nd century AD.
Enlightenment thinkers.Simone de Beauvoir: Trap: her 1949 book The Second Sex helped launch modern feminism, but she is a 20th-century existentialist, not part of the 18th-century Enlightenment.
Enlightenment thinkers.Epicurus: Trap: this Greek philosopher around 300 BC taught that the aim of life is calm and freedom from fear. Hellenistic, so far before the Enlightenment.

Happened in the Middle Ages.Black Death: The plague killed perhaps a third or more of Europe's people between 1347 and 1351, reshaping labor and society.
Happened in the Middle Ages.Crusades: A series of religious wars launched from 1095, aiming to take Jerusalem. The First Crusade captured the city in 1099.
Happened in the Middle Ages.Magna Carta: King John sealed it in 1215 at Runnymede, and the principle that even a king is bound by law still echoes today.
Happened in the Middle Ages.Norman Conquest: William of Normandy took England in 1066, which brought a French-speaking elite and thousands of French words into English.
Happened in the Middle Ages.Hundred Years' War: England and France fought on and off from 1337 to 1453, which actually lasted 116 years. Joan of Arc rose to fame in it.
Happened in the Middle Ages.Viking raids: They began around 793 AD with the attack on Lindisfarne monastery, and Norse raiders and settlers reshaped much of Europe.
Happened in the Middle Ages.Battle of Hastings: In 1066 William defeated King Harold, who is said, in later accounts, to have been killed by an arrow in the eye.
Happened in the Middle Ages.Wars of the Roses: Rival branches of the English royal family, York and Lancaster, fought for the crown in the 1400s until Henry Tudor won in 1485.
Happened in the Middle Ages.Peasants' Revolt: In 1381 English commoners marched on London to protest a poll tax, and the young Richard II met them, though Wat Tyler died.
Happened in the Middle Ages.Domesday survey: William the Conqueror ordered this great survey in 1086 to record who owned what, and it was so thorough it was likened to the Last Judgment.
Happened in the Middle Ages.French Revolution: Trap: it began in 1789, after the Middle Ages, in the modern era, and it overthrew the monarchy.
Happened in the Middle Ages.Thirty Years' War: Trap: it raged across Europe from 1618 to 1648, in the early modern period, and devastated much of Germany.
Happened in the Middle Ages.American Revolution: Trap: the colonies broke from Britain in the 1770s and 80s, well after the medieval era.
Happened in the Middle Ages.Spanish Armada: Trap: Philip II's fleet sailed against England in 1588, so it is Elizabethan, not medieval.
Happened in the Middle Ages.Great Fire of London: Trap: it began in a Pudding Lane bakery in 1666, which is early modern, and destroyed old St Paul's Cathedral.
Happened in the Middle Ages.Gunpowder Plot: Trap: Guy Fawkes and fellow plotters tried to blow up Parliament in 1605, an early modern conspiracy.
Happened in the Middle Ages.Napoleonic Wars: Trap: they took place from 1803 to 1815, long after the medieval age.
Happened in the Middle Ages.Trojan War: Trap: the legendary war belongs to the Greek Bronze Age, well before the Middle Ages, and is known through Homer.
Happened in the Middle Ages.Punic Wars: Trap: Rome fought Carthage in three wars between 264 and 146 BC, so this is antiquity, not the medieval world.
Happened in the Middle Ages.Boston Tea Party: Trap: colonists dumped tea into Boston Harbor in 1773, a prelude to the American Revolution.
Happened in the Middle Ages.Gold Rush: Trap: California's rush began in 1848, in the 19th century, and brought hundreds of thousands to the West.
Happened in the Middle Ages.Titanic sinking: Trap: it sank in April 1912, an event of the early 20th century.
Happened in the Middle Ages.Waterloo: Trap: Napoleon lost this battle in 1815, a 19th-century event that ended his rule.
Happened in the Middle Ages.Moon landing: Trap: Apollo 11, 1969. The Middle Ages ended about 500 years earlier.

Things that have wheels.Suitcase: Wheeled luggage only became common around 1970, when Bernard Sadow patented a rolling design, oddly late for a wheel-using species.
Things that have wheels.Office chair: Most have five legs, not four, because a five-point base resists tipping far better when you lean back.
Things that have wheels.Shopping cart: Invented in 1937 in Oklahoma by Sylvan Goldman, who watched shoppers stop buying once their baskets got heavy.
Things that have wheels.Skateboard: Early skateboards in the 1950s were made by nailing roller-skate wheels to a plank, and surfers used them for 'sidewalk surfing'.
Things that have wheels.Wheelbarrow: It's a lever as well as a wheel: the load sits close to the wheel, so you lift only a fraction of its weight.
Things that have wheels.Stroller: The first baby carriage was built in 1733 for a duke's children and was pulled by a goat or small pony.
Things that have wheels.Lawnmower: Edwin Budding invented it in 1830 in England, reportedly adapting a machine used to trim the nap on cloth.
Things that have wheels.Wheelchair: Wheelchair basketball and racing chairs are built with tilted wheels, which make sharp turns faster and more stable.
Things that have wheels.Bicycle: Early bikes had no pedals at all: the 1817 'running machine' was pushed along with your feet.
Things that have wheels.Roller skates: Inline skates were invented in the 1700s, yet the four-wheel 'quad' design took over once it let skaters steer by leaning.
Things that have wheels.Hospital bed: Its wheels have central locking brakes, and modern beds can tilt, raise, and lower to ease patient care.
Things that have wheels.Toy train: Model trains often run on rails of a standard 'gauge' set by size; O, HO, and N are named for their scale.
Things that have wheels.Hand truck: Often called a dolly, it works by shifting the load's weight onto the axle so one person can move a heavy appliance.
Things that have wheels.Sled: A trap: sleds slide on runners rather than rolling, which is why they work on snow where wheels would bog down.
Things that have wheels.Canoe: Canoes need no wheels because they float, and the oldest known one, from the Netherlands, is roughly 10,000 years old.
Things that have wheels.Snowboard: It has no wheels: the Snurfer, a 1960s toy, launched it, and snowboarding joined the Olympics in 1998.
Things that have wheels.Kayak: The word is Inuit, and traditional kayaks used sealskin stretched over a driftwood or whalebone frame instead of wheels.
Things that have wheels.Hammock: The word comes from a Taino term; sailors adopted hammocks because they swung with the ship and stayed level.
Things that have wheels.Bookcase: Heavy and stationary, a bookcase has no wheels, though library shelving sometimes rolls on tracks to save space.
Things that have wheels.Pogo stick: It bounces on a spring, not wheels, and the record for consecutive jumps on one is well over 200,000.
Things that have wheels.Stilts: Shepherds in France's marshy Landes region once walked on tall stilts to see over flocks and cross wet ground.
Things that have wheels.Ski: Skis glide on snow, not wheels, and the oldest known ski, found in Russia, is thought to be about 8,000 years old.
Things that have wheels.Surfboard: Hawaiian royalty once rode huge wooden boards, and modern foam-and-fiberglass boards have no wheels, just a fin or three.
Things that have wheels.Diving board: It's a fixed springboard, not a wheeled thing, and its flex stores energy that launches divers higher than a jump could.

Things with a trigger.Spray bottle: Squeezing the trigger works a tiny pump that forces liquid through a nozzle, which makes a mist rather than a stream.
Things with a trigger.Glue gun: Hot glue guns melt plastic sticks at around 120 degrees Celsius, and the trigger pushes the stick forward.
Things with a trigger.Nail gun: Nail guns use compressed air or gas to drive nails in a few milliseconds, which is far faster than any hammer swing.
Things with a trigger.Power drill: The trigger on many drills is variable speed, so pressing harder makes it spin faster.
Things with a trigger.Water pistol: Super Soakers were invented by NASA engineer Lonnie Johnson, who was working on a heat pump when he squirted a stream across his bathroom.
Things with a trigger.Caulk gun: The trigger moves a plunger forward in a ratchet, pushing a thick bead of sealant from the tube.
Things with a trigger.Gas pump nozzle: The nozzle trigger shuts off by itself when fuel hits a small sensor hole, which stops the tank overflowing.
Things with a trigger.Pressure washer: A trigger on the wand controls the spray, and the water can be strong enough to strip paint.
Things with a trigger.Leaf blower: A leaf blower's trigger controls the throttle, and some petrol models push air at well over 100 miles an hour.
Things with a trigger.Chainsaw: Chainsaws have a 'dead man' safety latch, and the trigger works only when the latch is pushed in.
Things with a trigger.Hammer: A hammer is a simple lever with no moving parts, which is why it has changed so little since the Stone Age.
Things with a trigger.Screwdriver: The Phillips head was designed so the driver would 'cam out' and slip rather than overtighten screws.
Things with a trigger.Wrench: Adjustable wrenches were patented in the 1800s, and the Swedish inventor Johan Petter Johansson later made the type used today.
Things with a trigger.Paint roller: The paint roller was invented in 1940 by Canadian Norman Breakey, and it spreads paint faster than a brush.
Things with a trigger.Whisk: A whisk has no trigger, though some electric versions do, and its loops are shaped to whip air into the mixture.
Things with a trigger.Pliers: Pliers squeeze with handles, and the handle is hinged rather than triggered.
Things with a trigger.Tape measure: The tape's curved cross-section keeps it rigid enough to stand out, then it rolls back into the case on a spring.
Things with a trigger.Spirit level: The bubble in a spirit level sits in alcohol, which doesn't freeze easily and flows quickly.
Things with a trigger.Crowbar: A crowbar is a simple lever and has no mechanism, so it needs no trigger.
Things with a trigger.Paintbrush: A paintbrush has no mechanism at all, and good ones hold paint among the bristles by capillary action.
Things with a trigger.Garden rake: A rake's tines gather leaves, and it's a simple tool with no moving parts or triggers.
Things with a trigger.Shovel: Shovels are among the oldest tools, and a trigger would only complicate the design.
Things with a trigger.Ladder: A ladder's rungs are just fixed crossbars, and you don't squeeze anything to use it.
Things with a trigger.Trowel: A trowel is a small hand shovel for planting, and it's the gardener's simplest tool.

Glands in the human body.Thyroid: The thyroid sets your metabolic pace, and it needs iodine, which is why salt is often iodized.
Glands in the human body.Adrenal: Adrenal glands sit atop each kidney and release adrenaline for the fight-or-flight response.
Glands in the human body.Pituitary: The pituitary is pea-sized but called the master gland because it signals many other glands.
Glands in the human body.Pancreas: The pancreas is both a digestive gland and a hormonal one, making insulin and digestive enzymes.
Glands in the human body.Sweat gland: Sweat glands number about two to four million over the body, and they mostly cool you through evaporation.
Glands in the human body.Salivary gland: Salivary glands make about a liter of saliva a day, and a bite of something sour makes them work harder.
Glands in the human body.Pineal: The pineal gland releases melatonin, the sleep hormone. Descartes once called it the seat of the soul.
Glands in the human body.Parathyroid: The parathyroid glands are four tiny glands behind the thyroid that control calcium levels in your blood.
Glands in the human body.Thymus: The thymus trains immune T cells and shrinks after puberty, so it's largest in children.
Glands in the human body.Tear gland: Tear glands sit above each eye and make the fluid that keeps the cornea moist.
Glands in the human body.Cornea: The cornea is the clear front of the eye. It's tissue and not a gland.
Glands in the human body.Femur: The femur is the thigh bone. It makes blood cells in its marrow, but it isn't a gland.
Glands in the human body.Tendon: A tendon joins muscle to bone, so it isn't a gland.
Glands in the human body.Aorta: The aorta is the body's largest artery and carries blood out of the heart, so it's a vessel, not a gland.
Glands in the human body.Spleen: The spleen filters blood and is an immune organ, but it makes no hormones, so it isn't a gland.
Glands in the human body.Kidney: The kidneys filter blood and make the hormone erythropoietin, but they're classified as organs, not glands.
Glands in the human body.Biceps: Biceps is a muscle in the arm, and not a gland.
Glands in the human body.Patella: The patella is the kneecap, a bone, so it's no gland.
Glands in the human body.Cochlea: The cochlea is the hearing organ of the inner ear, and not a gland.
Glands in the human body.Uvula: The uvula is a flap at the back of the throat, and not a gland, though it has mucus glands in it.
Glands in the human body.Trachea: The trachea is the windpipe, a tube for air, so it's not a gland.
Glands in the human body.Retina: The retina senses light at the back of the eye, so it's tissue rather than a gland.
Glands in the human body.Gallbladder: The gallbladder stores bile made by the liver. It's a sac, and the liver is the gland.
Glands in the human body.Appendix: The appendix is a small pouch off the large intestine, and it isn't a gland, though it holds immune tissue.

Restaurant kitchen brigade roles.Sous chef: French for 'under-chef', the second in command of the kitchen. They run things when the head chef is away.
Restaurant kitchen brigade roles.Chef de partie: Runs one station, such as sauces or fish. Also called a station chef, it's a core part of the classic brigade.
Restaurant kitchen brigade roles.Saucier: The sauce specialist, a prestigious station in classic French kitchens. Sauces are at the heart of French cuisine.
Restaurant kitchen brigade roles.Pâtissier: The pastry chef in a brigade, responsible for desserts and baked goods. The role often has its own area apart from the hot kitchen.
Restaurant kitchen brigade roles.Commis chef: A junior cook learning under a chef de partie. 'Commis' is French for 'trainee' or 'junior'.
Restaurant kitchen brigade roles.Garde manger: French for 'keeper of the food'. This station prepares cold dishes like salads, terrines and charcuterie.
Restaurant kitchen brigade roles.Poissonnier: The fish cook. The name comes from 'poisson', French for fish.
Restaurant kitchen brigade roles.Rôtisseur: Handles roasted, grilled and braised meats. The name comes from the French for roast.
Restaurant kitchen brigade roles.Chef de cuisine: The head of the kitchen, the 'executive chef' in many places. The word 'chef' simply means chief.
Restaurant kitchen brigade roles.Line cook: Works a single cooking station on the line. It's the backbone of the modern restaurant kitchen.
Restaurant kitchen brigade roles.Pastry chef: A baker of desserts and pastries, a specialist job. Pastry chefs often work separately from the hot line.
Restaurant kitchen brigade roles.Sommelier: A wine steward who works in the dining room, not the kitchen. It comes from an old French word for a pack-animal driver.
Restaurant kitchen brigade roles.Maître d': Short for 'maître d'hôtel', who manages the dining room and greets guests. They're front-of-house, not in the kitchen.
Restaurant kitchen brigade roles.Waiter: Serves tables in the dining room, so they aren't part of the kitchen brigade. Tipping customs vary widely by country.
Restaurant kitchen brigade roles.Busboy: Clears tables and resets them. This front-of-house job isn't in the kitchen brigade.
Restaurant kitchen brigade roles.Barista: Italian for 'bartender', it now means a coffee maker. It's a cafe role, not a kitchen post.
Restaurant kitchen brigade roles.Concierge: A hotel guest helper. The word is thought to stem from French for 'keeper of the candles'.
Restaurant kitchen brigade roles.Bellhop: A hotel porter who carries luggage. The name comes from the call bell hotels once used to summon them.
Restaurant kitchen brigade roles.Valet: Parks cars or serves a household. The word comes from French and relates to 'vassal'.
Restaurant kitchen brigade roles.Hostess: Greets guests and seats them in the dining room. It's a front-of-house role.
Restaurant kitchen brigade roles.Cashier: Handles payments, not cooking. The word comes from the French 'caisse', a money box.
Restaurant kitchen brigade roles.Doorman: Stands at the entrance, so he's a hotel or club role, not a kitchen one.
Restaurant kitchen brigade roles.Usher: Shows people to seats in theaters or weddings. The word comes from Latin for a door guard.
Restaurant kitchen brigade roles.Croupier: A casino dealer who runs table games. The word originally meant 'one who rides behind', from French.

Sorting algorithms.Bubble sort: It swaps neighbors again and again until the list settles, and it is mostly taught as an example of what not to use.
Sorting algorithms.Quicksort: Tony Hoare devised it in 1959 while working on machine translation, and it is still a standard choice in many libraries.
Sorting algorithms.Merge sort: John von Neumann described it in 1945, and it splits a list in halves, sorts each, and then merges them.
Sorting algorithms.Heapsort: It builds a heap and repeatedly pulls out the largest item, guaranteeing good worst-case speed without extra memory.
Sorting algorithms.Insertion sort: It works like sorting a hand of playing cards, and it is surprisingly quick on small or nearly sorted lists.
Sorting algorithms.Selection sort: It repeatedly finds the smallest remaining item and moves it to the front, always doing about the same work.
Sorting algorithms.Radix sort: It sorts numbers digit by digit without comparing them, which is how old punch-card sorting machines worked.
Sorting algorithms.Shell sort: Donald Shell published it in 1959, and it improves insertion sort by first comparing items that are far apart.
Sorting algorithms.Bogosort: It shuffles the list at random until it happens to be sorted, which is a joke algorithm that could take longer than the universe's lifetime.
Sorting algorithms.Timsort: Tim Peters wrote it for Python in 2002, and it is now used by Java and Android because real data is often partly ordered.
Sorting algorithms.Counting sort: It tallies how often each value appears, so it never compares items and runs fast when the range is small.
Sorting algorithms.Binary search: It finds an item in a sorted list by halving the range each time, but it finds things rather than sorting them.
Sorting algorithms.Hashing: It turns data into a fixed-size number, which makes lookups quick, and it is used to store passwords but not to sort.
Sorting algorithms.Recursion: A function that calls itself is a technique, not a sorting method, though merge sort and quicksort both use it.
Sorting algorithms.Compiler: It translates source code into machine code, and Grace Hopper built one of the first in the early 1950s.
Sorting algorithms.Linked list: Each item points to the next, so inserting is cheap, but it is a way to store data, not to order it.
Sorting algorithms.Stack: This last-in, first-out structure gives us the undo button, and it is a data structure, not a sort.
Sorting algorithms.Queue: First in, first out, like a line at a shop, and it holds data in order of arrival rather than sorting it.
Sorting algorithms.Big O: This notation describes how an algorithm's time grows with input size, so it measures sorts but is not one.
Sorting algorithms.Debugger: The word bug is older than computers, but Grace Hopper's team famously taped a real moth into a log in 1947.
Sorting algorithms.Encryption: It scrambles data to keep it secret, and sorting plays no part even though the idea goes back to Caesar.
Sorting algorithms.Binary tree: It stores items with up to two children per node, and with tree sort it can be used to sort, but it is not a sort itself.
Sorting algorithms.Garbage collection: Invented for Lisp around 1959, it frees memory that a program no longer uses, with no ordering involved.
Sorting algorithms.Dijkstra's algorithm: Edsger Dijkstra devised it in 1956 to find shortest paths in a graph, and he reportedly designed it in about twenty minutes.

Nintendo console accessories.Zapper: The NES light gun, made famous by Duck Hunt, works by briefly flashing targets white and checking whether the gun sees them.
This toy robot of 1985 was made to make the NES feel like a toy, which helped Nintendo sell it to wary US shops after the 1983 crash.
Nintendo console accessories.Wii Balance Board: It senses your weight and balance with four sensors, and it was the controller for Wii Fit, which sold tens of millions of copies.
Nintendo console accessories.Wii Remote: Its infrared sensor and motion sensing let you swing it like a racket, and it made Wii Sports a hit with non-gamers.
Nintendo console accessories.Nunchuk: It plugs into the Wii Remote, and its name is a nod to the martial arts weapon the two-piece pair resembles.
Nintendo console accessories.Rumble Pak: The N64 plug-in shook the controller using AA batteries and debuted with Star Fox 64.
Nintendo console accessories.Game Boy Camera: The 1998 grayscale camera took photos at 128 by 112 pixels, and it is now beloved by lo-fi photographers.
Nintendo console accessories.Joy-Con: These detachable Switch controllers contain an infrared camera and high-definition rumble, and they famously can develop drift.
Nintendo console accessories.Wii Zapper: This 2007 plastic shell held a Wii Remote and Nunchuk, and it was bundled with Link's Crossbow Training.
Nintendo console accessories.Transfer Pak: This N64 accessory let Game Boy cartridges plug in, famously linking Pokemon Red and Blue to Pokemon Stadium.
Nintendo console accessories.Expansion Pak: It doubled the N64's memory from 4 MB to 8 MB, and some games like Donkey Kong 64 required it.
Nintendo console accessories.Game Boy Printer: This 1998 thermal printer printed photos and stickers on tiny paper rolls, and it had no ink at all.
Nintendo console accessories.Kinect: This is Microsoft's Xbox motion sensor, so it belongs to another console maker, not Nintendo.
Nintendo console accessories.EyeToy: Sony's PlayStation 2 camera of 2003 turned your body into the controller, so it is not a Nintendo accessory.
Nintendo console accessories.PlayStation Move: Sony answered the Wii Remote with it in 2010, so it is a PlayStation accessory, not a Nintendo one.
Nintendo console accessories.DualShock: Sony added vibration and analog sticks with this 1997 PlayStation pad, which is not from Nintendo.
Nintendo console accessories.Sixaxis: This wireless PS3 controller of 2006 had motion sensing but no rumble, which is a Sony accessory.
Nintendo console accessories.Xbox Elite pad: Microsoft's premium pad has swappable thumbsticks, and it is made for Xbox, not Nintendo consoles.
Nintendo console accessories.Steam Controller: Valve's 2015 pad used two trackpads in place of sticks, and it is meant for PCs rather than Nintendo.
Nintendo console accessories.Sega Activator: This 1993 Genesis floor ring was meant to turn your body into a controller, and it was famously hard to use.
Nintendo console accessories.Dreamcast VMU: Sega's memory card had its own tiny screen and could be played as a handheld, and it is not Nintendo.
Nintendo console accessories.DualSense: The PS5 controller has adaptive triggers that resist your finger, which makes it a Sony product.
Nintendo console accessories.Sega Menacer: Sega's 1992 Genesis light gun was a bazooka-style rival to the Zapper, but it is not from Nintendo.
Nintendo console accessories.PocketStation: Sony's 1999 PlayStation memory card also served as a tiny handheld with a screen, and it was a Japan-only item.

Shakespeare tragedies.Hamlet: At roughly 4,000 lines it is Shakespeare's longest play, and the title role is one of the biggest parts in drama.
Shakespeare tragedies.Macbeth: The shortest of his tragedies, and actors superstitiously call it 'the Scottish play' because saying the name in a theatre is said to bring bad luck.
Shakespeare tragedies.Othello: Iago, not Othello, has the most lines; the play follows a Moorish general in Venice undone by jealousy.
Shakespeare tragedies.King Lear: For about 150 years audiences saw Nahum Tate's rewrite with a happy ending, until the original returned in the 1800s.
Shakespeare tragedies.Romeo and Juliet: The lovers die within days of meeting, and Juliet is not yet 14, a youth Shakespeare took from his source poem.
Shakespeare tragedies.Julius Caesar: Caesar is killed in act three, yet the play carries his name, and Brutus has far more lines.
Shakespeare tragedies.Antony and Cleopatra: A tragedy that swings between Rome and Egypt, ending with Cleopatra's death by an asp's bite.
Shakespeare tragedies.Coriolanus: It follows a Roman general who despises the public he needs; he is banished and joins Rome's enemies.
Shakespeare tragedies.Titus Andronicus: Shakespeare's bloodiest play includes a revenge in which two sons are baked into a pie.
Shakespeare tragedies.Timon of Athens: Likely co-written with Thomas Middleton, and seemingly unfinished, it follows a generous man ruined by false friends.
Shakespeare tragedies.Twelfth Night: A comedy of shipwreck, mistaken twins and a cross-dressing heroine, not a tragedy despite its gloomy Malvolio.
Shakespeare tragedies.The Tempest: Often classed as a romance rather than a tragedy; it is among Shakespeare's last plays and ends in forgiveness.
Shakespeare tragedies.As You Like It: A pastoral comedy known for the 'All the world's a stage' speech; nobody important dies.
Shakespeare tragedies.Henry V: A history play with the 'band of brothers' speech before Agincourt, not a tragedy.
Shakespeare tragedies.Love's Labour's Lost: A comedy that famously ends without the usual weddings, with the lovers told to wait a year.
Shakespeare tragedies.The Winter's Tale: A romance with the most famous stage direction in theatre, 'Exit, pursued by a bear', so it isn't a tragedy.
Shakespeare tragedies.Measure for Measure: One of the 'problem plays', a dark comedy with a tragic edge, but it is classified as a comedy.
Shakespeare tragedies.Doctor Faustus: Christopher Marlowe's tragedy about a scholar who sells his soul to the devil; it is not by Shakespeare.
Shakespeare tragedies.The Duchess of Malfi: John Webster's Jacobean tragedy of revenge and madness is a dark rival of Shakespeare's, not his.
Shakespeare tragedies.Oedipus Rex: Sophocles' Greek tragedy was written about two thousand years before Shakespeare, so it is not his.
Shakespeare tragedies.The Comedy of Errors: Shakespeare's shortest play, a farce about two sets of twins, so a comedy rather than a tragedy.
Shakespeare tragedies.Henry VIII: A history play likely co-written with John Fletcher; the Globe burned down during a 1613 performance.
Shakespeare tragedies.Faust: Goethe's German drama of a man bargaining with the devil is not Shakespeare's.
Shakespeare tragedies.The Crucible: Arthur Miller's 1953 play about the Salem witch trials is a tragedy, but by an American writer.

Things that spin.Spinning top: Tops are one of the oldest toys, found in ancient Mesopotamia, and they stay upright thanks to gyroscopic effects while spinning fast.
Things that spin.Fidget spinner: The toy exploded in popularity in 2017, though a patent for a similar spinning toy was filed in 1993 by Catherine Hettinger.
Things that spin.Ceiling fan: Ceiling fans cool people by moving air across skin, not by lowering the air temperature, so leaving one on in an empty room wastes power.
Things that spin.Merry-go-round: The carousel's name comes from Italian words for 'little battle', as it began with knights' riding exercises, before it turned into a ride.
Things that spin.Wind turbine: The longest turbine blades now exceed 100 meters, and their tips can spin at speeds over 250 kilometers per hour.
Things that spin.Record player: A needle in a vinyl groove reads microscopic bumps shaped by the sound, and the standard LP spins at 33 and a third rotations per minute.
Things that spin.Ferris wheel: The first, built by George Ferris for the 1893 Chicago World's Fair, stood about 80 meters tall and carried over 2,000 riders at once.
Things that spin.Helicopter rotor: A helicopter's spinning blades work as rotating wings, and the pilot changes their pitch to climb, descend or tilt in any direction.
Things that spin.Dreidel: The four-sided spinning top is played at Hanukkah, and each side shows a Hebrew letter standing for 'a great miracle happened there'.
Things that spin.Pinwheel: A pinwheel spins when wind pushes on its angled vanes, and the same principle powers the huge turbines at wind farms.
Things that spin.Revolving door: Theophilus Van Kannel patented the revolving door in 1888, and the design blocks drafts so a building saves on heating.
Things that spin.Salad spinner: Centrifugal force flings water off the greens toward the basket's walls, the same physics as a washing machine's spin cycle.
Things that spin.Planet Earth: Earth spins once every 24 hours, roughly 1,670 kilometers per hour at the equator, and the spin is slowing very slightly over time.
Things that spin.Seesaw: A seesaw tilts up and down on a pivot, a lever in action, and the two riders never complete a turn.
Things that spin.Playground slide: A slide runs straight downhill, and a spiral slide comes closest to circling around, but you do not spin.
Things that spin.Swing: A swing moves back and forth like a pendulum, and a child swings at a rate set by the chain length, not by how hard they push.
Things that spin.Pendulum: Galileo noticed that a swinging pendulum takes the same time for small swings, and clocks used this idea for centuries.
Things that spin.Elevator: An elevator travels in a straight line, and in 1853 Elisha Otis showed off a safety brake that stops it falling when the rope snaps.
Things that spin.Trampoline: The trampoline gets its name from the Spanish trampolin, a diving board, and the inventor George Nissen first built one in 1930s.
Things that spin.Ladder: A ladder just stands or leans, and a rope ladder is among the oldest climbing tools, though none of them rotate.
Things that spin.Pogo stick: A pogo stick bounces on a spring instead of spinning, and it was patented in Germany in the 1920s, becoming a craze worldwide.
Things that spin.Metronome: A metronome's arm swings back and forth like a pendulum, and Beethoven was an early fan of its tempo marks.
Things that spin.Rocking chair: A rocking chair moves back and forth on curved runners, and Benjamin Franklin is often credited with popularizing the rocker in America.
Things that spin.Hammock: The word hammock comes from a Taino word, and Columbus's crew saw Caribbean people sleeping in them, then adopted them as bunks.

Italian vehicle brands.Ferrari: Enzo Ferrari ran Alfa Romeo's racing team before founding his own car company in 1947, and its prancing horse logo is on every car.
Italian vehicle brands.Lamborghini: Lamborghini began as a tractor maker, and Ferruccio Lamborghini built supercars after a spat with Enzo Ferrari over a clutch.
Italian vehicle brands.Maserati: Maserati's trident logo comes from the Neptune statue in Bologna, and the firm was founded there in 1914 by the Maserati brothers.
Italian vehicle brands.Fiat: Fiat, Italian for let it be done, is short for Fabbrica Italiana Automobili Torino, and the Fiat 500 became an icon of postwar Italy.
Italian vehicle brands.Alfa Romeo: Alfa Romeo's name merges Anonima Lombarda Fabbrica Automobili with Nicola Romeo, and its serpent badge comes from Milan.
Italian vehicle brands.Lancia: Lancia's Delta Integrale won six straight World Rally Championships for manufacturers, in the late 1980s and early 1990s.
Italian vehicle brands.Pagani: Pagani is a small Italian maker of hypercars, founded by Horacio Pagani, an Argentine who once worked at Lamborghini.
Italian vehicle brands.Ducati: Ducati makes motorcycles in Bologna, famous for the desmodromic valve system and the red Italian look of its bikes.
Italian vehicle brands.Vespa: Vespa means wasp in Italian, named for its buzzing engine and narrow waist, and Piaggio launched it in 1946.
Italian vehicle brands.Piaggio: Piaggio, Italian, began as a ship-fitting company and built aircraft before launching the Vespa scooter in 1946.
Italian vehicle brands.Aprilia: Aprilia is an Italian motorcycle maker known for road racing success, and it was bought by Piaggio in 2004.
Italian vehicle brands.Abarth: Abarth tunes small Fiats, and the company's scorpion badge reflects founder Carlo Abarth's zodiac sign, Scorpio.
Italian vehicle brands.Iveco: Iveco makes trucks, buses, and vans in Turin, and its name stands for Industrial Vehicles Corporation.
Italian vehicle brands.Porsche: Porsche is German, not Italian, and its 911 has been built in Stuttgart since the 1960s.
Italian vehicle brands.Peugeot: Peugeot is French, and its lion logo dates from the 1850s, when the family sold saws and other steel tools.
Italian vehicle brands.Seat: Seat is Spanish, founded in 1950 with Fiat's help and based near Barcelona, and it's now owned by Volkswagen Group.
Italian vehicle brands.Renault: Renault is French, and it's among the oldest car makers still operating, going back to 1899.
Italian vehicle brands.Jaguar: Jaguar is British, and it began in 1922 as the Swallow Sidecar Company, making motorcycle sidecars.
Italian vehicle brands.Koenigsegg: Koenigsegg is Swedish, not Italian; the hypercar maker works from a former air force hangar at Ängelholm.
Italian vehicle brands.McLaren: McLaren is British, and it was founded by New Zealand racing driver Bruce McLaren and has won the Formula One constructors' title many times.
Italian vehicle brands.Aston Martin: Aston Martin is British, and its name comes from the Aston Hill hillclimb, and James Bond made its DB5 the most famous spy car.
Italian vehicle brands.Skoda: Skoda is Czech and began in 1895 making bicycles, and it's now part of Volkswagen Group.
Italian vehicle brands.Triumph: Triumph is a British motorcycle brand, and Steve McQueen made the Triumph famous in The Great Escape.
Italian vehicle brands.Opel: Opel is German, founded by Adam Opel, who started with sewing machines and later built bicycles.

Types of boat.Canoe: Canoes are among the oldest boats, and the oldest known one, found in the Netherlands, is roughly 10,000 years old.
Types of boat.Kayak: Inuit hunters built kayaks from sealskin stretched over wood or whalebone frames, and the word means hunter's boat.
Types of boat.Yacht: The word yacht comes from the Dutch jacht, meaning hunt, and Dutch light ships were first used for chasing pirates.
Types of boat.Sailboat: Sailboats can sail against the wind by angling their sails, and they can't sail directly into it; they zigzag in a maneuver called tacking.
Types of boat.Ferry: Ferries have crossed water for thousands of years, and Staten Island's, in New York, carries tens of thousands of commuters for free.
Types of boat.Tugboat: Tugs are small but extremely powerful for their size, and they can nudge ships many times their weight in and out of port.
Types of boat.Barge: A barge is a flat-bottomed cargo boat that's often pushed or towed, and a single river barge can carry as much as dozens of trucks.
Types of boat.Dinghy: A dinghy is a small boat, often the tender carried by a bigger yacht, and its name comes from a Hindi word for a small boat.
Types of boat.Catamaran: A catamaran has two hulls, and Polynesians sailed them across the Pacific long before Europeans arrived.
Types of boat.Gondola: Venetian gondolas are all painted black, as a 16th century law required, and are built asymmetrically so they glide straight when rowed on one side.
Types of boat.Rowboat: Rowers face backward, so you can't see where you're going, which is why the sport has a coxswain to steer in competitive crews.
Types of boat.Trawler: A trawler fishes by dragging a net, and it has long been a mainstay of the North Sea fishing industry.
Types of boat.Junk: The Chinese junk has stiff, battened sails that fold up like a fan, and the design dates back around two thousand years.
Types of boat.Dhow: The dhow is a traditional Arabian sailing ship with triangular lateen sails, and it carried trade across the Indian Ocean for centuries.
Types of boat.Sleigh: A sleigh glides on runners over snow, not water, and Santa's famous one is pulled by reindeer.
Types of boat.Toboggan: The word toboggan comes from an Algonquian language, and it's a runnerless sled for snow, not water.
Types of boat.Rickshaw: The word rickshaw comes from Japanese jinrikisha, meaning human-powered vehicle, and it runs on wheels, not water.
Types of boat.Tram: Trams run on rails along city streets, and Hong Kong's double-decker ones have run since 1904, but they never float.
Types of boat.Zeppelin: A zeppelin is an airship, not a boat, though it was a vessel of the sky, and its engines sat in gondolas hung beneath.
Types of boat.Monorail: A monorail rides one beam above ground, and Seattle's, built for the 1962 World's Fair, still runs; it never sails.
Types of boat.Segway: The Segway is a self-balancing scooter that stays upright with gyroscopes, and it was launched in 2001.
Types of boat.Trolley: A trolley is a streetcar or a cart, and the word trolley comes from the pole that took power from overhead wires.
Types of boat.Caravan: The word caravan once meant a group of desert travelers, and now it means a towed home on wheels.
Types of boat.Wagon: A wagon has four wheels, and pioneer wagons crossing the American plains were pulled by oxen, not pedaled.

Things usually found in a bathroom.Bathtub: Archimedes famously shouted 'Eureka' in a bath, and a standard tub can hold around 150 litres.
Things usually found in a bathroom.Shower: The shower is thought to have been used in ancient Greece, and modern pressurized ones date from the 1800s.
Things usually found in a bathroom.Toilet: The flush toilet was popularized by Thomas Crapper's company in Victorian England, but earlier ones date to Sir John Harington in 1596.
Things usually found in a bathroom.Sink: The first ones in homes were basins, and the tap you turn was fitted with hot and cold from separate pipes in old buildings.
Things usually found in a bathroom.Towel rail: Heated towel rails dry towels, and in cold countries they also warm the room.
Things usually found in a bathroom.Toothbrush: The first bristle toothbrush appeared in China around 1498, using hog hair, and nylon bristles came in 1938.
Things usually found in a bathroom.Shampoo: The word comes from the Hindi 'champo', meaning to massage, and was brought to Britain from India in the 1800s.
Things usually found in a bathroom.Plunger: The rubber plunger was patented in the late 1800s, and its suction works best when a seal is formed.
Things usually found in a bathroom.Loofah: It's not a sponge from the sea, but the dried fibrous fruit of a gourd plant, which you can also eat young.
Things usually found in a bathroom.Toilet paper: Modern rolls date to 1857 in the US, and the ancient Chinese used paper for it in the 6th century.
Things usually found in a bathroom.Medicine cabinet: Bathroom mirrors with storage are common, though experts note that heat and humidity make a bathroom a poor place for medicine.
Things usually found in a bathroom.Oven: It belongs in the kitchen, and a bathroom oven would be a steamy surprise.
Things usually found in a bathroom.Toaster: A toaster plus a bath is a deadly mix, so they stay far apart, and it belongs in the kitchen.
Things usually found in a bathroom.Fridge: The refrigerator is a kitchen appliance, and the earliest domestic ones appeared in the early 1900s.
Things usually found in a bathroom.Sofa: It lives in the living room, and the word comes from Arabic 'suffa' meaning bench.
Things usually found in a bathroom.Bookshelf: It belongs in a study or living room, as steam would warp the books.
Things usually found in a bathroom.Dishwasher: It's a kitchen machine, invented by Josephine Cochrane in 1886, so not in the bathroom.
Things usually found in a bathroom.Crib: A baby's bed for the nursery, not the bathroom.
Things usually found in a bathroom.Coffee maker: A kitchen device, and not usually found near the toilet.
Things usually found in a bathroom.Dining table: A dining room piece, where food is eaten, so thankfully not in the bathroom.
Things usually found in a bathroom.Piano: It goes in a living or music room, and though it sounds nice in the shower, you won't find a piano.
Things usually found in a bathroom.Kettle: A kitchen item, and its steam has no place beside the toilet.
Things usually found in a bathroom.Lawn mower: It belongs in the garage or shed, not the bathroom.
Things usually found in a bathroom.Grandfather clock: This tall pendulum clock stands in a hall or living room, and the name comes from a 1876 song.

Car body styles.Sedan: Sedan likely comes from a 17th-century enclosed chair carried by two men, and the name now covers the classic four-door car with a separate trunk.
Car body styles.Hatchback: A hatchback's rear door swings up with the rear window, which lets a small car carry surprisingly bulky loads.
Car body styles.Convertible: Convertibles have folding roofs, and many modern ones use electric motors to stow the top in about 20 seconds.
Car body styles.Coupe: Coupe comes from French for cut, since the style cut back the rear seating of a carriage into a sleek two-door shape.
Car body styles.Station wagon: Station wagons got their name because they were used to carry passengers and luggage to railway stations.
Car body styles.Minivan: The minivan boom began in 1984 with the Dodge Caravan and Plymouth Voyager, which shaped the family car for decades.
Car body styles.SUV: SUV stands for sport utility vehicle, and the Jeep Wagoneer of 1963 is often called a forerunner of the type.
Car body styles.Roadster: Roadsters are two-seat open cars, and the Mazda MX-5 Miata is the best-selling one ever made.
Car body styles.Crossover: A crossover has an SUV's look but a car's frame, which usually makes it lighter, and it dominates sales today.
Car body styles.Estate: In Britain, an estate is what Americans call a station wagon, with a long roof and a big rear cargo space.
Car body styles.Cabriolet: The word originally named a light horse-drawn carriage with a folding hood that bounced over roads, which the car style borrowed.
Car body styles.Saloon: In British English a saloon is simply a sedan, and the same word in the Wild West meant a bar.
Car body styles.Limousine: The name comes from the French region Limousin, where the shepherds' hooded cloaks were said to inspire the driver's covered compartment.
Car body styles.Tanker: A tanker is a heavy truck or ship carrying liquids, so it is a type of cargo vehicle, not a body style for ordinary cars.
Car body styles.Moped: A moped's name blends motor and pedal, and its small engine and pedals mark it as a motorbike, not a car shape.
Car body styles.Rickshaw: Rickshaws are pulled by a person or powered by small engines, and the form is a different vehicle from car bodies.
Car body styles.Tandem: A tandem is a bicycle for two riders in a row, and the word is Latin for at length, so not a car style.
Car body styles.Bobsled: A bobsled is an ice sport vehicle with steel runners, with no relation to car body shapes.
Car body styles.Caboose: The caboose is the last car on a freight train where crew once rode, so it is a railroad car, not a car body style.
Car body styles.Dinghy: A dinghy is a small boat, and its name comes from a Hindi word for a little boat.
Car body styles.Trolleybus: A trolleybus draws power from overhead wires, so it is a bus style rather than a car body type.
Car body styles.Glider: A glider is an engineless aircraft, so it has no place among car body shapes.
Car body styles.Segway: The Segway is a two-wheeled self-balancing scooter, not a car body style.
Car body styles.Tuk-tuk: The tuk-tuk is a three-wheeled taxi, so it isn't classed among normal car body types.

Toyota models.Corolla: Over 50 million Corollas have been sold since 1966, making it the best-selling nameplate in car history.
Toyota models.Camry: Camry comes from the Japanese 'kanmuri', meaning crown, and it was the best-selling car in America for much of the 2000s.
Toyota models.Prius: The Prius, launched in Japan in 1997, was the first mass-produced hybrid car, and its name is Latin for 'to go before'.
Toyota models.Yaris: Toyota said the Yaris name draws on Charis, a Greek goddess of grace, mixed with the German word 'ja'.
Toyota models.Land Cruiser: The Land Cruiser was renamed in 1954 to compete with Land Rover, and its reputation for toughness made it a favorite in the outback and across Africa.
Toyota models.RAV4: RAV4 stands for Recreational Active Vehicle with 4-wheel drive, and in 1994 it was one of the first compact crossovers.
Toyota models.Hilux: A Hilux survived being crashed, drowned and set on fire on Top Gear, and still started, cementing its reputation as indestructible.
Toyota models.Supra: The Supra, spun off from the Celica, gained fame in pop culture when an orange one starred in the first Fast and Furious film.
Toyota models.Celica: Celica is Latin-derived for 'heavenly', and the sporty coupe ran from 1970 until 2006.
Toyota models.Tacoma: The Tacoma is a midsize pickup, and has been the top seller in its class in the US for many years.
Toyota models.Tundra: The Tundra is Toyota's full-size pickup, built in Texas to take on Ford's F-150 and Chevy's Silverado.
Toyota models.Civic: The Civic is Honda's, and it competes with the Corolla but isn't a Toyota.
Toyota models.Accord: The Accord is Honda's family sedan, a rival to the Camry rather than a Toyota.
Toyota models.Altima: The Altima is Nissan's midsize sedan, built in Tennessee and Mississippi.
Toyota models.Sentra: The Sentra is Nissan's compact sedan, and its name is not Toyota-related at all.
Toyota models.Micra: The Micra is Nissan's small hatchback, and Nissan builds it for Europe.
Toyota models.Leaf: The Leaf is Nissan's electric car, and since 2010 it has been among the best-selling EVs ever.
Toyota models.Outback: The Outback is Subaru's rugged wagon, sold since 1994, so it isn't Toyota's.
Toyota models.Impreza: The Impreza is Subaru's compact, famous for its rally-winning versions in the 1990s.
Toyota models.Elantra: The Elantra is Hyundai's compact sedan, and its name is not from Toyota.
Toyota models.Sonata: The Sonata is Hyundai's midsize sedan, and it's named for the musical form.
Toyota models.Lancer: The Lancer is Mitsubishi's, and the Evolution version became a rally legend.

Palindromes.Level: A five-letter palindrome which also describes a spirit level, the bubble tool builders use.
Palindromes.Radar: The word is itself an acronym, for radio detection and ranging, and it reads the same backward.
Palindromes.Civic: Honda's compact car shares its name with this palindrome meaning relating to a town or citizens.
Palindromes.Kayak: This Inuit-origin word is a palindrome, and the original boats were made from seal skins stretched over a frame.
Palindromes.Madam: A polite address that is also the classic palindrome in Adam's greeting: Madam, I'm Adam.
Palindromes.Refer: Read it from either end and it's the same; it comes from the Latin referre, to carry back.
Palindromes.Rotor: The spinning part of helicopters and engines, and a palindrome in English.
Palindromes.Racecar: A rare compound palindrome, in which the car has the same spelling forward and back.
Palindromes.Noon: Midday is a palindrome, and the word comes from the Latin nona hora, the ninth hour, which moved earlier over centuries.
Palindromes.Stats: Short for statistics, and a four-letter palindrome.
Palindromes.Tenet: A principle or doctrine; the title of Christopher Nolan's 2020 film, which plays on palindromes and time inversion.
Palindromes.Deed: A legal document or an act, and a palindrome.
Palindromes.Solos: A word for performances by one, which reads the same backward.
Palindromes.Lever: It looks palindromic, but backward it spells revel, a different word; true palindromes read identically both ways, like level.
Palindromes.Radio: A near miss with radar: read backward it becomes oidar, which is no word at all, so it fails the mirror test.
Palindromes.Civil: It shares its first letters with civic, but backward it's livic, so only the one with matching ends is a palindrome.
Palindromes.Kayaks: Adding a plural s ruins kayak: the mirror image is skayak, proving that a palindrome is fragile to small changes.
Palindromes.Madame: The French honorific looks close to madam, but the extra e breaks the symmetry; backward it reads emadam.
Palindromes.Refers: Refer is a palindrome, but the added s makes it sreferr backward, a clear trap for quick readers.
Palindromes.Roster: It hides the word rot at its start, and a mirror image fails: backward it reads retsor.
Palindromes.Raceway: Racecar is a palindrome, but raceway isn't, since backward it reads yawecar.
Palindromes.Noun: It looks like noon, but backward it spells nuon, because the middle letters differ.
Palindromes.State: Stats is a palindrome, but state reads etats backward; a single letter changes the answer.
Palindromes.Tenants: It echoes tenet in sound and look, yet backward it reads stnanet, so it fails.
